from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
out=Path('tmp/pdfs'); out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
print('Pages:',len(r.pages))
texts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
 text=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
 (out/f'page-{i:02}.txt').write_text(text)
 texts.append(f'\\n\\n=== PAGE {i} ===\\n{text}')
(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(texts))
print(''.join(texts[:3]))
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: editing emotion-bearing content while retaining the source scene. Figures 1, 6, and S11 show plausible semantic transformations beyond global color changes, using only a source image and target emotion at inference.

EmoPair is a potentially useful resource, comprising 331,595 emotion-labeled InstructPix2Pix pairs and 6,949 generated pairs. The manuscript attributes the underlying datasets and methods and links a release of code, models, and data.

The substantial human study reports 136 participants and 24,480 trials, with randomized presentation and attention checks. Overall preferences of approximately 56% against EmoEdit and 53% against LMS provide evidence of practical benefits beyond classifier-based evaluation.

The supplementary material strengthens the assessment through human-annotated emotional regions and CrossTest evaluation using separately trained predictors. The disclosure of facial artifacts, limitations of categorical emotions, and potential misuse is constructive; consent, ethics approval, and compensation are also reported.
weaknesses: The architectural contribution is not convincingly isolated. In Table 2, the EmoPair-fine-tuned text-conditioned variant with iterative emotion inference already achieves 50.24% ESMI, compared with 51.56% for the complete method; without iteration, that baseline scores 5.85%. Thus, most improvement comes from iterative inference. Human evaluations of this critical ablation are needed to establish the benefit of the emotion encoder and alignment loss. Describing cosine alignment to instruction embeddings as human-like neuro-symbolic reasoning also exceeds the demonstrated mechanism.

Comparison fairness remains uncertain. EmoEditor can perform up to 30 editing iterations, while comparable inference budgets are not established for the main baselines, and runtime or iteration distributions are not reported. Several instruction-based baselines receive only a single emotion word, although the paper itself explains why such prompts are ineffective. LMS is a useful stronger comparison, but evaluating it and EmoEdit with comparable iterative selection would better separate model improvements from additional computation.

ESMI does not adequately establish the claimed balance between emotional effectiveness and content preservation. The same predictor labels training data, selects generated images, and supplies the main emotion score; human-annotated masks do not remove this dependence. CrossTest usefully mitigates this concern, but the architectural ablations are not repeated under independent evaluation. Furthermore, S_str rewards increasing changes inside the emotional mask without directly measuring absolute preservation of neutral regions or semantic coherence. The human study evaluates emotional preference, not source-content fidelity.

Important mathematical and training details require clarification. Under the conventional KL definition, KLD(e_s, e_oh) is infinite for a soft distribution against a one-hot target; adding epsilon to the final denominator does not resolve this. Section 3.2 also defines the corrupted latent from the source image and never explicitly introduces the paired edited target into the denoising objective, which reads as source reconstruction. These may be specification errors rather than implementation failures, but corrected definitions are necessary. Learning rate, batch size, training duration, and inference sampling settings are also missing.

Dataset quality is insufficiently characterized for a central contribution. Most pairs receive automatic emotion labels, while the reported human correction exercise covers only 300 examples from the generated subset. Label accuracy, annotation agreement, correction frequency, and emotion-transition distributions are not reported. An EPAS/EPGS ablation would establish whether the newly generated pairs contribute beyond relabeling existing editing data.

Some claims are broader than the evidence. Same-valence, neutral-image, and multi-emotion generalization receive qualitative examples rather than systematic evaluation. Figure S9 reports only 47% preference against LMS for generating positive emotions, qualifying the broad superiority narrative. The positioning of the task and dual-branch architecture as novel also needs sharper differentiation from the cited EmoEdit and standard image/text-conditioned editing architectures.
